column4: The source section points to this ruling itself: it names bound oaths, عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ, and their kaffāra is feeding ten poor, freeing a neck, or fasting three days when unable. It supplies the legal passage from oath to feeding and release.

The source section’s dictionary form tahillat is explicit here: Allah prescribes the dissolution of your oaths, تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ. This directly grounds the knot-and-release image in a divine ruling.

The section cites this expiation: after the zihar utterance, the man must perform تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ before the spouses touch again. It gives a second concrete setting for release as repair after speech.

This is the continuation of 58:3: if the man cannot free someone, he performs فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا. Its own contribution is the food branch, joining expiation to the section’s feeding passage.

The source section’s root y-m-n appears in الْأَيْمَانَ بَعْدَ تَوْكِيدِهَا; this verse commands keeping Allah’s covenant and not breaking oaths after confirmation. It gives the binding side of the section’s knot image.

The warning against becoming like the woman who unravels her yarn after firm spinning, نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا, is an explicit image of undoing what was made secure; 16:91 supplies the oath context, while this verse supplies the unraveling simile.

The source section’s knot-and-untying account is made literal in Moses’s prayer to loosen a knot from his tongue, وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي. Here release enables speech to be understood, a precise nonlexical parallel to loosening an oath-knot.

The verse gives Job a way to act without breaking his oath: take a bundle in the hand and strike with it, “and do not break your oath,” وَلَا تَحْنَثْ. It is a divine solution to a sworn obligation, complementing the section’s account of prescribed oath-release.

This names a concrete oath not to approach one’s wife, يُؤْلُونَ مِن نِّسَائِهِمْ, gives a four-month term, and says return is open. It makes the oath’s resolution and the alternative of remaining bound a lived legal scene.

The source section’s root y-m-n appears in عُرْضَةً لِّأَيْمَانِكُمْ; this verse says not to make Allah an obstacle to righteousness, reverence, or peacemaking. It marks the boundary the image needs: an oath should not block the good that the section presents as feeding and mercy.

Here people are told not to swear off giving, وَلَا يَأْتَلِ, to relatives, the poor, and emigrants, and are urged to pardon. This reverses the garden owners’ oath to keep the poor out and aligns oath-release with renewed generosity.

After taking a covenant, Allah promises, لَأُكَفِّرَنَّ عَنكُمْ سَيِّئَاتِكُمْ, to cover the people’s sins if they fulfill its terms. This links a binding commitment to the source section’s expiatory sense of root ك ف ر.

The source section’s root k-f-r appears in يُكَفِّرُ عَنكُم مِّن سَيِّئَاتِكُمْ: this verse joins giving charity to the poor with Allah’s covering of some misdeeds. It directly meets the section’s claim that provision for the needy can cover the evil of a spoken wrong.

The verse uses the source section’s root ك ف ر, يُكَفِّرَ, for covering believers’ sins and says their light runs before them and at their right hands. It brings the section’s expiation and right-hand associations into one final-judgment scene.

At the Day of Gathering, Allah covers believers’ sins, يُكَفِّرْ عَنْهُ سَيِّئَاتِهِ, and admits them to gardens. This is the positive outcome on the same root ك ف ر as the section’s kaffāra; 64:10 supplies the contrasting fate.

This verse pairs Allah’s covering believers’ sins, وَيُكَفِّرَ عَنْهُمْ سَيِّئَاتِهِمْ, with their admission to gardens, using the same expiatory root ك ف ر as the source section. Ayah 48:6 supplies the opposite group, so this row contributes the saved side of that contrast.

At the time of an inheritance division, الْقِسْمَةَ, relatives, orphans, and the poor are present and are to be given something. This concretizes the source section’s dictionary account of qasāma as oaths distributed among a dead person’s kin, while joining division to its needy recipients.

For accidental killing, this verse joins تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُؤْمِنَةٍ with compensation to the victim’s family and fasting if freedom is unavailable. It is not the qasāma procedure, but it concretely meets the source’s slain-kin definition and 90:13’s freeing-neck image.

This account of righteousness gathers giving wealth to kin, orphans, and the poor, وَفِي الرِّقَابِ, keeping pledges, and patience in hardship. It closely gathers the source section’s release, feeding, and moral passage in one ayah.

The prescribed shares of charity include the poor, needy, and those in bondage, فِي الرِّقَابِ. This connects the section’s allocation sense of qasāma with its specific movement from the oath to feeding and freeing.

Abraham asks, رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا آمِنًا, that this town be secure and that its people receive fruit. It ties the source section’s oath over “this city” to the provision that the section’s passage turns toward the hungry.

This calls the Quraysh to worship رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ, identifying the sanctuary in the immediate context of 106:4’s feeding against hunger. It supplies the local setting that joins the city oath to food provision.

The verse says Allah fed the Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear, أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ. It connects the city named in the oath with the section’s feeding on a day of hunger; 106:3 identifies the sanctuary.
This is another divine oath sequence whose final object is “this secure city,” وَهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ. The connection to 90:1 is the same sacred city, not merely the oath formula.
The divine formula فَلَا أُقْسِمُ introduces an oath by the stars’ settings, repeating the distinctive opening formula the section notes at 90:1.
This next ayah calls the oath in 56:75 عظِيمٌ, a great oath. Its contribution is to interpret the oath’s stature, completing the link begun there.
This repeats the section’s opening formula لَا أُقْسِمُ, here swearing by Resurrection Day. The shared form makes this a direct parallel in the act of divine oath-making.
This continues the same formula with an oath by the self-reproaching soul. Its own contribution is a second object of the repeated oath, completing the sequence opened in 75:1.
This uses the same label as 90:18, أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ, for the people of the right. The exact group-name grounds the source section’s link from al-maymana to the right side.
The verse again names أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ and opens their description. It gives a repeated right-side designation using the source section’s root y-m-n and ties it to a favorable group.

Within the right-hand group’s description opened in 56:27, this verse assigns the preceding garden scene to أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ. Its contribution is to identify that reward as belonging to the right-hand group.
At death, the verse again classifies a person as among أَصْحَابِ الْيَمِينِ. This applies the source section’s right-side label to the final encounter.
The next ayah greets the person, فَسَلَامٌ لَّكَ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الْيَمِينِ, with peace from the companions of the right. Its contribution is the welcome attached to the group named in 56:90.
The verse identifies a saved group as أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ, a repeated right-side designation that clarifies the favorable sense of the source section’s al-maymana.
Here the record is given in the right hand, بِيَمِينِهِ. It makes the source section’s hand-sense of yamin concrete in a judgment scene.
This again gives the record to a person in the right hand, بِيَمِينِهِ, and promises an easy reckoning. It connects the section’s right-hand sense of yamin to favorable judgment.

The verse says people will be given their records in the right hand, بِيَمِينِهِ, at the gathering. This is another concrete right-hand sign of outcome that grounds the source section’s yamin/hand association.
The believers’ light runs before them and at their right hands, وَبِأَيْمَانِهِمْ. This gives the source section’s right-hand association a visible image of guidance and safety.
The righteous give food, وَيُطْعِمُونَ الطَّعَامَ, to the needy, orphan, and captive. This is a direct social scene parallel to the source section’s feeding of the poor and freeing of the neck.

This ayah distinguishes idle oaths, اللَّغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ, from what hearts deliberately bind. That boundary clarifies why the section’s image of a tied oath and its expiation concerns an intended bond, not every passing utterance.

The verse warns against making أَيْمَانَكُمْ دَخَلًا between people, because feet may slip after having been firm. That reverses the section’s oath as a binding that can be released through a divinely prescribed remedy.

The command not to trade Allah’s covenant, عَهْدَ اللَّهِ, for a small price gives a material-gain reversal: the garden owners’ oath is aimed at keeping the harvest for themselves, while this verse names covenant as worth more than immediate gain.

The source section’s root y-m-n appears with Allah’s covenant, عَهْدَ اللَّهِ وَأَيْمَانَهُمْ, which this verse says people sell for a small price, losing a share of the Hereafter. It reverses the oath’s role as a path toward the successful group.

The source section’s root y-m-n appears in the hypocrites’ shield-oaths, أَيْمَانَهُمْ جُنَّةً, which they use to block Allah’s path. This is a cover that conceals wrongdoing, reversing the section’s expiation that covers a broken oath’s harm.

This repeats the shield-oath image, أَيْمَانَهُمْ جُنَّةً, from the source section’s y-m-n root, now used to obstruct Allah’s way. It is the reversal in the hypocrites’ own passage: oath as concealment rather than repair.

The next ayah says they believed and then disbelieved, كَفَرُوا, and their hearts were sealed. Beside 63:2’s oath-shield, it puts the source section’s root ك ف ر in its denial sense against its expiation-and-covering sense.

The verse says they swear they did not speak, though they did speak a word of disbelief, كَلِمَةَ الْكُفْرِ. It joins a false oath to the source section’s root ك ف ر, showing the contrary case of a word and oath that are not repaired.

This says those who disbelieve, كَفَرُوا, and deny Allah’s signs remain in the Fire. Its own contribution is the condemned group and sealed outcome, matching the section’s contrast at 90:19–20; 64:9 gives the covered-sin counterpart.

This verse describes the opposing group and the Fire, جَهَنَّمَ, prepared for them. It contributes the negative side of the believers’ covering and garden outcome in 48:5, paralleling the section’s right/left and fire ending.
This names the opposing group as أَصْحَابُ الْمَشْأَمَةِ. It supplies the left-side boundary paired with 56:8 and with the section’s companions of the right versus the left.

The opposite person receives the record in the left hand, بِشِمَالِهِ. Its own contribution is the reversal of the right-hand reception in 69:19, matching the section’s contrast between the right and left groups.
This contrasts the right-hand recipient in 84:7 with one given the record وَرَاءَ ظَهْرِهِ. The ayah provides the opposite side of the right-hand judgment image.
This says the person whose record came from behind will enter سَعِيرًا. Its own contribution is the punishment for the negative judgment outcome, echoing the sealed Fire in the section’s final ayah.
The verse reproaches people for not urging one another to feed the poor, عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ. It is the direct opposite of the food passage that the source section presents as a way through.
The denier of the judgment pushes away the orphan, يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ. This reverses the section’s care for the orphan and its account of the oath leading toward mercy.
The same denier does not urge feeding the poor, عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ. It is a precise contrary scene to the section’s food for the hungry.
The condemned person does not urge feeding the poor, طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ. This is a direct opposite of the food that the source section makes the passage through expiation.

The garden owners swear, إِذْ أَقْسَمُوا, to harvest in the morning. The source section explicitly contrasts this human oath, whose aim is to keep the poor from the garden, with the oath that opens a way through feeding.
They make no exception, وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ, to their plan. This contributes the unqualified, closed character of the oath whose aim is disclosed in 68:24.

At dawn they call one another, فَتَنَادَوْا مُصْبِحِينَ, to carry out the harvest plan sworn in 68:17. This row contributes the move from oath to morning action in the garden owners’ reversal of the section’s food passage.

They tell each other to go early to their crop, اغْدُوا عَلَىٰ حَرْثِكُمْ, if they mean to harvest it. This supplies the concrete action the oath in 68:17 anticipated, in the plan that excludes the poor.
The owners set out وَهُمْ يَتَخَافَتُونَ, speaking privately. This contributes the concealed execution of the exclusionary plan stated in 68:24, reversing the section’s feeding passage.
The plan is stated: no poor person is to enter the garden that day, أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ... مِسْكِينٌ. This is the exact reversal of the section’s oath-to-food passage.
They go out غَدَوْا عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ, resolved and thinking they have power over the harvest. This completes the execution of the plan sworn in 68:17 to reserve the garden for themselves.

After their exclusionary oath, a blast from their Lord, طَائِفٌ مِّن رَّبِّكَ, visits the garden while they sleep. It begins the reversal of the harvest they intended to reserve; the section’s linked scene is 68:17 and its aim is stated in 68:24.
The garden is found ruined, كَالصَّرِيمِ, so the planned private harvest disappears. This is the outcome reversing the oath in 68:17 and withholding plan in 68:24.

After the plan sworn in 68:17 and exclusion stated in 68:24, they see the ruined garden and say إِنَّا لَضَالُّونَ, thinking they have lost their way. This is their first recognition that the promised harvest has vanished.
They correct themselves: rather, بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ, they have been deprived. Its own contribution is to name the loss that reverses the plan in 68:17 and the exclusion in 68:24.

After the oath of 68:17 and the exclusion stated in 68:24, this verse identifies the garden’s loss as punishment and warns that عَذَابَ الْآخِرَةِ is greater. It completes the reversal of the owners’ plan to hoard the harvest.

This immediately precedes 66:2: the Prophet is asked لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ مَا أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكَ, and the next ayah prescribes release of oaths. This verse gives the particular self-imposed restriction to which that release responds.

The verse identifies the zihar saying as مُنكَرًا مِّنَ الْقَوْلِ and false; 58:3 names its expiation. Its contribution is to identify the spoken wrong that the section’s freeing and feeding imagery can cover.

After 2:226’s oath concerning marital relations, this verse gives the other path: if the couple decides on divorce, Allah hears and knows. It completes the boundary between returning from the oath and proceeding to separation.

For killing game during pilgrimage, this verse names كَفَّارَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ or fasting. The offense differs from a broken oath, but it gives another concrete Quranic legal passage where expiation is carried by food and fasting.

The source section’s root ح ل ل appears as حَلَلْتُمْ for coming out of pilgrimage consecration, after which hunting is permitted. It is a different legal release from an oath, but concretely shows the root’s movement from restriction to release.

The verse names the knot of marriage, عُقْدَةَ النِّكَاحِ, and sets a limit on resolving it until the prescribed term. It is not an oath, but it gives a concrete legal knot beside the source section’s image of an oath-bound knot and its loosening.

After captives are firmly bound in battle, the verse allows release, فِدَاءً, or pardon. This is not oath-expiation, but its concrete movement from bondage to release echoes the freeing-neck branch of the image.

This legal procedure uses sworn testimony, فَيُقْسِمَانِ بِاللَّهِ, when death intervenes and explicitly mentions a near relative. It is not qasāma, but its death-and-kin setting gives a concrete Quranic counterpart to the source section’s dictionary account of oaths among a slain person’s kin.

The source section’s root ق س م also occurs in the statement that Allah apportioned livelihoods among people, قَسَمْنَا. In its ordinary allocation sense, the verse adds a provision-and-distribution parallel to the image’s feeding of the poor.

This verse distributes public wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor, and travelers, كَيْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ مِنكُمْ, so it will not circulate only among the rich. It gives a specific economic reversal to the garden owners’ oath excluding the poor from a share.

The verse uses the source section’s root ك ف ر, لِيُكَفِّرَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ, for covering the worst of what people did and rewarding their best. This is the same covering sense that the section draws from kaffāra, though here the covered deeds are general rather than a broken oath.

The verse explicitly asks whether there is an oath, قَسَمٌ, in the preceding signs for a person of understanding. It makes the source section’s named root ق س م a question about how signs warrant an oath, rather than merely repeating the formula.

After the exclusion plan in 68:24 fails, they say سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا and admit wrongdoing. This may echo the image’s movement from a wrongful utterance toward return, though the verse does not prescribe the oath-expatiation law discussed in the section.

The ayah says that whoever waives a claim in retaliation receives expiation, فَهُوَ كَفَّارَةٌ لَّهُ. This joins the source section’s root k-f-r with a concrete homicide-and-pardon ruling, complementing its qasāma definition about oaths among a slain person’s kin.

After 2:84’s covenant not to shed blood or expel one another, this ayah describes them doing both, then ransoming their captives, تُفَادُوهُمْ. It links a broken bond and kin-related bloodshed to release, while reversing the source section’s use of oath and freeing as a path toward care.

This retaliation ruling lets the victim’s brother forgive and calls for compensation to be paid fairly, فَمَنْ عُفِيَ لَهُ مِنْ أَخِيهِ شَيْءٌ. It supplies a concrete Quranic scene of a slain person’s kin receiving a release from retaliation, adjacent to the section’s qasāma definition.

The verse gives the guardian of a person killed unjustly authority, لِوَلِيِّهِ سُلْطَانًا, while forbidding excess in retaliation. This grounds the source section’s qasāma reference to the slain person’s close kin in a Quranic rule about their standing.

The covenant here forbids shedding one another’s blood and expelling one another, مِيثَاقَكُمْ. Ayah 2:85 describes its violation and the later ransoming of captives; this row contributes the original binding that makes that reversal concrete.

This verse protects the orphan’s property, مَالَ الْيَتِيمِ, commands just speech even when a relative is concerned, and ends by commanding fulfillment of Allah’s covenant. It gathers the orphan, kin, and binding obligation that the section brings together through qasāma and feeding.

The verse joins care of the orphan’s property, مَالَ الْيَتِيمِ, to the command to fulfill the covenant, وَأَوْفُوا بِالْعَهْدِ. This is a specific pairing of the section’s vulnerable kin and binding-promise themes.

This warns that those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire and will burn in a blaze. It sharply reverses the section’s feeding and care for the orphan, and joins that reversal to its final fire image.

A designated share of the gains is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, وَلِذِي الْقُرْبَىٰ وَالْيَتَامَىٰ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ. This gives another concrete allocation of resources to the kin and poor who appear in the source section’s qasāma definition and feeding passage.

This verse places feeding a poor person, فِدْيَةٌ طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ, as a compensation alongside a fasting obligation. Its arrangement differs from the source section’s oath expiation, where fasting is the fallback, but it gives a specific parallel between fasting and feeding.

Following 76:8’s feeding of the needy, this ayah gives the feeders’ stated motive: they feed for Allah’s sake, لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ, seeking neither payment nor thanks. That motive contrasts with the garden owners’ self-serving oath and completes the feeding scene with its own contribution.

The verse encourages a contractual route out of bondage, فَكَاتِبُوهُمْ, and calls for material help from what Allah has provided. This is a concrete emancipation scene that complements the source section’s freeing-neck branch, though it is not an oath expiation.

This ayah says they do not honor the orphan. It adds the neglected recipient to the nearby rebuke in 89:18 about failing to urge food for the poor, directly reversing the source section’s orphan-and-feeding passage.

After 89:17–18’s neglect of the orphan and poor, this verse says they devour inheritance voraciously, وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا. It reverses the source section’s image of a share distributed among a slain person’s kin and the garden owners’ attempt to reserve the harvest.

This continues the same rebuke by naming their intense love of wealth, وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا. Its own contribution is the attachment that makes the exclusionary garden oath and withheld provision legible.

After Moses asks in 20:27 for the knot of his tongue to be loosened, this ayah states the purpose: that they understand his speech, يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي. It completes a precise image of release applied to speech, beside the source section’s oath-knot and its untying.

This ayah names the companions of the left, أَصْحَابُ الشِّمَالِ, the opposing group whose counterpart appears in the source section’s closing division between the fortunate side and the condemned side.

The left group’s scene continues with scorching wind and boiling water, فِي سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ. Its own contribution is the concrete punishment completing the group label in 56:41 and echoing the sealed Fire at the end of the source surah.
The next ayah adds a shade of black smoke, وَظِلٍّ مِّن يَحْمُومٍ, to the left group’s punishment begun in 56:41. This further detail extends the contrast with the source section’s right-hand group.

This says that the smoke-shade is neither cool nor beneficial, لَا بَارِدٍ وَلَا كَرِيمٍ. It completes the deprivation in 56:41–43, a specific opposite to the section’s passage through feeding and mercy.

This asks about the one who denies the Judgment, يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ, framing the orphan-repelling and refusal to urge food in 107:2–3. Its own contribution is to identify the stance behind those contrary acts, matching the section’s contrast with those who reject Allah’s signs.

This concludes the same short portrait by saying they withhold small assistance, وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ. It adds a concrete form of deprivation beyond the failure to urge food in 107:3, opposite the section’s provisions for the needy.

This ayah says the condemned person did not believe in Allah, لَا يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ; 69:34 then specifies that he did not urge food for the poor. This row contributes disbelief as the stance behind that specific withholding.

In the conditional warning begun in 69:44 about inventing words against Allah, this ayah says the Messenger would be seized بِالْيَمِينِ. The source section’s root y-m-n is here the literal right hand, a distinct but pointed counterpart because its discussion joins oath and hand.

This states the condition of fabricating words against Allah, تَقَوَّلَ عَلَيْنَا بَعْضَ الْأَقَاوِيلِ, before the right-hand seizure in 69:45. It contrasts the source section’s true divine oath with false speech attributed to God.

The warning continues with cutting the aorta, الْوَتِينَ, after the seizure in 69:45. This is the consequence completing that false-speech scene, a severe reversal of the section’s remedial feeding and freeing after a broken oath.
